turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the tenth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things up top. A tanker war in the Gulf turned into a shooting war, and oil broke a hundred dollars.
A million-dollar pay rise landed in Singapore the same week a relief cheque did. [wry] The optics wrote themselves.
[deadpan] We don't say that phrase on this show, Theo.
[laughs] Noted. And the whole book today hangs on one word — the premium. What a thing costs, and whether it's worth it.
Start with the Gulf, because it moved everything else. Over five days the United States and Iran traded fire at sea.
Wait — actual strikes? Not the drone-and-warning stuff from last week?
Actual strikes. On the eighth, US Central Command sank five Iranian crude tankers — four in the Gulf of Oman, one near Kharg Island.
[exhales] Five tankers.
It says the crews were warned off first, and no American personnel were hurt. Then, at dawn on the ninth, Iran hit back.
Hit back where?
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it struck two US vessels and more than a dozen tankers, and hit an airbase in Jordan with ballistic missiles.
[curious] And is that confirmed?
This is where you print both sides. Central Command says no US warship was hit and every attempt failed. Jordan says it shot down eighteen of twenty missiles, two fell in open ground, no casualties.
So the claim of hitting sheltered aircraft is Tehran's, and it's denied.

Denied. And the price did the rest of the talking. Brent crude crossed a hundred dollars for the first time since July — about a hundred dollars and forty-four cents. Saudi Arabia condemned a deadly strike on a tanker in the strait, so the neighbours are getting pulled in too.
[thoughtful] Up how much?
Roughly nine per cent in five days. This is day one hundred and ninety-four of a war that started back in February.
Okay, give me the three-capital version — how does each side tell it?

Tehran frames the US as the aggressor enforcing an illegal blockade. Washington projects control — deterrence delivered, not a war widened. Doha, Al Jazeera, leads with the escalation and the regional cost.
And the sceptic? Somebody must think a hundred-dollar oil doesn't last.
The bear case is spare capacity. Analysts at S and P Global argue the Gulf could cover a total loss of Iran's exports, and many still see Brent averaging around eighty-six dollars this year.
[skeptical] Except the spare capacity sits inside the same Gulf that's now on fire.
That's the rebuttal, yes. Goldman calls a hundred and twenty dollars plausible if exports stay choked — while its own base case still has oil falling to eighty-five by year end.
Hold that thought, because it runs straight into the money block. What about Ukraine?
Briefly. The three-day pause that let two US envoys shuttle between Moscow and Kyiv expired on the eighth. Overnight, Russia fired one hundred and sixty-six drones and thirty-two cruise missiles.
[sighs] So the talks went nowhere.
No ceasefire, no meeting scheduled. Kyiv's foreign minister put it plainly — the missiles speak louder than the words on diplomacy.
Right. The money block. This is where the oil actually bites, isn't it?
It's the whole story of the day. One barrel of oil, and three central banks tightening into it at once.
[curious] Three at once? That's rare.
Very. The European Central Bank is priced almost certain to hike to two point five zero per cent — today, in fact, the same day we print.
And the Fed?
A genuine coin-flip. Futures put a quarter-point hike at about fifty-nine per cent for the fifteenth and sixteenth, after the chair, Kevin Warsh, said there's still work to do on inflation.
A hike. Not a cut. [drawn out] People forget that's even on the menu.
And the switch is tomorrow's number. American inflation for August lands Friday — headline reaccelerating on energy, even as the core cools toward two point four per cent.
So oil pushes the headline up, the banks lean hawkish, and yields climb.
The ten-year Treasury sits near a three-year high, about four point seven seven per cent. Name the regime: an oil-shock reflation, havens bid, risk assets under pressure.
What does that do to a boring balanced portfolio? The classic sixty-forty?

No cushion this week. Rising real yields hit shares and bonds together — the all-world tracker capped near a hundred and ninety-five, the global bond fund down on the month. Positive correlation, which is the opposite of what you want.
And the two wild cards — gold and bitcoin?

They split. Gold near a record, about four thousand three hundred and sixty-eight dollars, taking the war-and-haven bid. Bitcoin around seventy-eight thousand and sliding — trading as a pure risk asset.
[thoughtful] So the safety money went to bullion and the yen, not to crypto.
Not this week. The Bank of Japan is leaning toward another hike too, and the yen firmed on it — so the haven trade this week is gold and the yen, full stop.
And bitcoin just sat in the risk-off bucket with the shares.
It did. And this is education, not advice — but that's the read for an all-world-plus-bonds holder: the diversifier isn't diversifying, and the digital-gold story took the week off.
Now weave Singapore in, because the same squeeze shows up locally.

It does. The lead is political salaries. On Monday the Government accepted the pay review, and it reached the floor of Parliament — a member of parliament's allowance rises to eighteen thousand five hundred dollars a month, from thirteen thousand seven hundred and fifty, effective the fifteenth of October.
And the Prime Minister?
Up about sixty-four per cent, to roughly three point six million dollars a year.
[gasps] In the same week as a cost-of-living payout?
The very same week. Four hundred to six hundred dollars reached two point four million people, against a national median income of five thousand seven hundred and seventy-five dollars a month.
[exhales] Yeah. That's a hard sell.
The Prime Minister said he'll donate his increment to charity for five years. A political scientist warned it still risks reading as tone-deaf.
Here's the premium again, though — you pay ministers the market rate to keep the service clean. That's the bet.
It's a defensible bet on paper. The trouble is it's paid in trust, and the electorate re-prices it every time the cheque is read aloud.
Quick hits on the island?

The haze is back — air quality crossed into unhealthy for the first time since October of twenty twenty-three. And the year's last flat launch offers about seven thousand nine hundred and seventy homes.
Good. Now the fun part — the desks that actually spend money well. Technology first.
Europe bought itself an artificial-intelligence champion. The Paris lab Mistral raised three billion euros, led by Samsung.
Samsung? The chip and memory giant?
The same. It values Mistral above twenty-one billion euros — the largest equity round in European tech history. And the money goes into owning data centres, not renting them.
[curious] Why does owning matter?
Because in the sovereignty game the defensible thing is the concrete and the power contract — not the model, which anyone can download.
And the sceptic line?
The revenue's about four hundred million dollars against a twenty-one-billion valuation. You're paying for a buildout and a bet, not for booked profit.
For the home-lab crowd — anything they can actually run?
Alibaba dropped a strong new open model, Qwen three-point-eight Flash-Next. It's brilliant — and it lands exactly as memory prices go vertical.
[skeptical] How vertical?
A thirty-two-gigabyte memory kit that cost eighty to a hundred and twenty dollars late last year now runs about four hundred. Analysts see another forty to fifty per cent before year end.
[sighs] So the buy-once move is —
Buy the memory now, not the model. The model will still be free in six months. The memory won't be cheaper.
The Kit. Give me the gadget.
Android glasses arrived on your face. XREAL made its Aura official — see-through lenses, a seventy-degree field of view, Google's assistant built in, under fifteen hundred dollars.
[excited] Finally. What's the catch?
The compute lives on a cable to a puck in your pocket. So after a decade of promising to cut the cord, they put one back on your face.
[chuckles] Of course they did. Is it shipping?
No. Ten thousand reservations, a deposit, a fall window — a promise, not a purchase. Wait for a price and a review.
And the Atelier — this is the buy-it-once desk. Today?
The weekender bag. The one holdall you buy once for a flight to Tokyo. And the word leather hides a four-tier con.
[amused] Teach me.

Full-grain is the whole top of the hide — it ages beautifully. Top-grain is sanded and sprayed, and wears through. Genuine leather is a marketing floor. Bonded is dust glued to a backing. And the stitch matters — a hand saddle-stitch stays put when it's cut, a machine stitch unravels like a ladder in a stocking.
And in our climate?

Here's the twist — the pretty veg-tanned leather drinks water. In eighty-two per cent humidity you want a chrome-tanned hide or a tough nylon, and you avoid the laminated fabrics that delaminate in the heat.
Give me the honest tiers.
A hundred and sixty dollars buys a genuine buy-once bag from GORUCK. Filson's rugged twill duffle is around four hundred and twenty-five, with a lifetime warranty.
And the grail?
Seven hundred to sixteen hundred buys leather that becomes an heirloom — Saddleback, Lotuff, Frank Clegg. Above that, you're paying for a name.
[skeptical] Name a name.
A Louis Vuitton Keepall is nineteen hundred and ninety dollars — and the body is coated canvas, not leather. That's the logo tax, in one bag.
The premium that buys nothing. And the Good Life keeps the theme going, doesn't it?
Perfectly. Chopard launched a chronograph with a Geneva Seal and a flyback movement — genuine high watchmaking — for about thirty-six thousand five hundred euros. Twenty-five pieces.
[thoughtful] So what's the catch this time?
The case is steel. The movement earns the premium; the metal doesn't. You can see under a loupe exactly what your money bought — which is more than a logo ever shows you.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Come on, this one's fun. Today it's DJing. Bedroom to booth.
And it's cheaper to start than people think. A controller and a free app — under five hundred dollars, all in.
What actually hooks people?
The first clean transition. Two records locked, the bass swapped, and nobody hears the seam. [warmly] That's the hit.
So what do I buy?
The starter almost everyone recommends is the DDJ-FLX four, about two hundred and ninety-nine dollars. It does ninety-five per cent of what a beginner needs, for years.
And the club stuff — the big glowing decks?
Those are the CDJ three thousands, about twenty-five hundred dollars each. A booth is two of them plus a mixer — call it eight thousand dollars.
[gasps] Eight thousand? In a bedroom?
And the community's own verdict is blunt — that's a flex, not a need. A standalone gives you the same workflow for a third of the money.
What's genuinely new in the hobby?

The deck learned to split a song in half. The software now pulls a vocal off a record live — instant acapellas, mashups on the fly. That's the real shift. And streaming plays straight off the hardware now, which is convenient right up until you realise you're renting your crate.
[amused] And the purists are furious about the sync button, I assume?

Endlessly. But the grown-up take is that sync is just a tool — selection, phrasing and reading a room matter far more, and the professionals all use it. There's also a whole turntablist lane, the classic Technics decks, if you want to scratch.
And the sceptic — because there's always one.

[wry] Gear-acquisition syndrome. New models every year, each implying you're one purchase from being good. You aren't. And your streamed record crate vanishes the day you stop paying the subscription.
[chuckles] Renting your own music. Okay — the body and the culture, quick round.
Fitness has a gift for busy people. A Harvard study of a hundred and forty-seven thousand adults found the strength-training sweet spot is ninety to a hundred and twenty minutes a week.
[curious] And after that?
Nothing. No extra benefit past two hours. Two sessions of about forty-five minutes gets most of the payoff. It's the rare study that tells you to stop paying.
General guidance, not medical advice — but I'll take it. Culture?
Venice claps for fourteen minutes. Martin McDonagh's new film drew the festival's longest ovation, but the top prize isn't decided until Saturday the twelfth.
So don't trust anyone who names a winner today.
Don't. And a footnote for scale — Spider-Man crossed two point four billion dollars, now the third biggest film ever made.
For the family desk?
Singapore's bringing in age checks for social media — under-thirteens off accounts on six named platforms. But it's twenty twenty-seven law, so nothing changes this term.
[thoughtful] So the lever a parent actually has right now is —
Sleep. Park the phone at night. That's the best-evidenced thing, and it costs nothing.
And the diary — anything to book?
The Grand Prix, ninth to eleventh of October — Marina Bay's first-ever sprint weekend, with The Killers and Lana Del Rey on the stages. And Bruno Mars tickets go on general sale on the fourteenth.
[warmly] Alright. Bring us home. The long read.
Malaysia. The nasi lemak, paid in three.
[curious] Paid in three?
Buy Now, Pay Later. In the West it finances a splurge. In Malaysia the average instalment is about ninety-one ringgit — roughly twenty US dollars — for groceries, formula, fuel.
So people are financing dinner.

Financing dinner. And it scaled fast — two hundred and forty-three million transactions last year, worth twenty-one billion ringgit, up seventy-eight per cent. Three apps hold most of it, sitting right inside the shopping checkout.
[thoughtful] And the killer number?

In one survey, more than half of users said they have no other credit at all. It's become the working overdraft for people the banks skipped — a small monthly figure that doesn't feel like debt, which is exactly the design.
[exhales] That's a different thing entirely from a shopping toy.
It's shadow welfare, by checkout button. The state pulls a fuel subsidy, and an app quietly offers to split the higher bill into three. The two aren't unrelated.
Is there a precedent?
South Korea, two thousand and three. A credit instrument sold as democratisation, handed out without underwriting — and it ended in a crisis, one in six working Koreans delinquent.
[thoughtful] And Malaysia's doing it differently?

That's the whole argument. Korea deregulated its way into the crash. Malaysia is trying to regulate its way around one — a brand-new commission, affordability checks, while this is still a rounding error in household debt.
Regulate before, not after. [warmly] That's genuinely rare.
It is. When the Financial Times writes it up in three weeks, you'll have heard it here — and you'll know the one number that decides which story it becomes.
Which is?
Not the transaction count. Whether the people paying for dinner in three had any other way to pay at all.
[pause] The premium you pay for having no other choice. That's the cruellest one in the book.
It is. That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
